brief: The 5 memory patterns for AI agents — when to use vector, kv, episodic, or none at all.

slots.body: Agents forget by default. The right memory layer—vector, KV cache, episodic, or none—determines recall depth, latency, and cost. Choose the pattern that matches your task horizon.
Every request is independent. There is no context retention between calls, making this the fastest and cheapest option for single-turn tasks.
slots.card1Body: Single-turn classification, entity extraction, or image captioning where prior context never matters.
slots.card2Body: Stateless agents scale horizontally but cannot hold a conversation without external memory injection.

slots.body: The entire conversation history lives inside the prompt. It is simple but burns tokens fast and hits context limits on long sessions.
slots.card1Body: Multi-turn chat, few-shot examples, and tasks where recent history is more important than distant facts.
slots.card2Body: Once the token ceiling is reached, older messages are dropped or summarized, causing information loss.

slots.body: Embeddings compress knowledge into a searchable index. The agent retrieves top-K chunks to augment the prompt with relevant long-term facts.
slots.card1Body: Large knowledge bases, documentation Q&A, and domains where exact recall of specific text matters.
slots.card2Body: Retrieval quality depends on chunk size, overlap, and embedding model alignment with the query distribution.

slots.body: Key-value attention states are cached after the first forward pass. Subsequent tokens reuse them, slashing latency and compute for long contexts.
slots.card1Body: High-throughput conversational agents and streaming completions where low time-to-first-token is critical.
slots.card2Body: Cache eviction strategies trade off between GPU memory pressure and the cost of recomputing attention from scratch.

slots.body: Agents store structured traces of past actions, decisions, and outcomes. Memory is replayed to improve future reasoning and avoid repeated mistakes.
slots.card1Body: Autonomous tool-use agents, multi-step workflows, and self-improving systems that learn from trial and error.
slots.card2Body: Without summarization or importance scoring, episodic logs grow unbounded and eventually drown the retrieval signal.

slots.body: Match memory depth to task horizon. Stateless for speed, context for chat, vectors for facts, KV for throughput, and episodic for learning.
slots.card1Body: Architects designing agent systems who must balance recall accuracy, infrastructure cost, and user experience.
slots.card2Body: Production agents often compose two or more memory layers rather than relying on a single pattern in isolation.

slots.body: Start with none, add vectors for knowledge, and layer episodic traces once your agent begins to loop.
slots.quote: MEMORY TURNS TOOLS INTO TRUE AGENTS
